meta.title: Methodology
meta.description: How the numbers are made: per-90 metrics, position-scoped percentiles, role fits and similarity - and what each of them does not claim.

title: Methodology
description: How raw match data becomes percentiles, scores, roles and rankings — and the limits of what those outputs support.

supplied.title: Which metrics the provider actually supplies
supplied.checked: Every metric below was checked against real recorded responses rather than against the provider's documentation, and the arithmetic of each was reproduced against the provider's own published per-90 figures where it publishes one.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.providers: Performance data comes from a match-data provider. Player identity, market values, contracts and transfer history come from the public Transfermarkt dataset. The site itself is never scraped.
sources.identity: The two sources use different player identifiers, so they are linked by an identity resolution step combining normalised name, date of birth, nationality, club and position, which records a confidence score for every match. Low-confidence matches are not linked automatically; they are held for manual review.

per90.title: Per-90 metrics
per90.body: Raw counts are divided by actual minutes played and scaled to 90 minutes, so a substitute and an ever-present are comparable. Percentage metrics such as pass completion and duel success are ratios of attempts, not per-90 rates.

percentiles.title: Percentiles and comparison context
percentiles.why: A raw per-90 figure is hard to read without knowing what is normal. Every metric is therefore also expressed as a percentile within a comparison population: a player at the 92nd percentile ranks above 92% of that group.
percentiles.alwaysOneOf: The comparison population is always one of:
percentiles.scopeCompetition: position group within a single competition and season, the default;
percentiles.scopeSelected: position group across a selected group of competitions;
percentiles.scopeAll: position group across every competition currently covered.
percentiles.shown: The population in use is displayed next to the number. It is never hidden, because a percentile without its reference group is not interpretable.

allLeagues.title: What an all-leagues percentile is a rank against
allLeagues.definitionBefore: The second percentile column ranks a player's
allLeagues.definitionAfter: against every player-season the dataset currently serves in their position. That is the whole definition, and it is deliberately a rank of what was observed rather than an estimate of what a player would do over a full season.
allLeagues.snapshotBefore: The competitions loaded at any moment are at different points in their seasons, because they do not start in the same month. On the snapshot this was last measured on, nine of 44 competitions contained a player who had reached a full season's minutes, and
allLeagues.snapshotAfter: of the players came from the other 35. The median player in Italy's top flight had 36 minutes; in South Korea's, 1,057. Both are in the same population.
allLeagues.extremeBefore: A per-90 figure from one match is as extreme as the data allows, and that shows in the distribution. A player with under 180 minutes reaches the top tenth of an all-leagues metric
allLeagues.extremeMiddle: of the time; a player with a full season does so
allLeagues.extremeAfter: of the time. Chance would give both 10%.
allLeagues.notAdjustedEmphasis: The percentile is not adjusted for any of this.
allLeagues.notAdjustedRest: It is not adjusted for season maturity, not adjusted for league strength, and not adjusted for how much evidence stands behind the player's own figure. Those are reported separately — as the composition of the comparison population, as minutes, and as a sample band — because an adjustment folded into a published number is one a reader cannot check.
allLeagues.bothAtOnce: So a player can honestly show a low all-leagues percentile and a full season of minutes at the same time. The percentile describes where their observed value sits in the observed distribution; the sample describes how much football produced that value. They answer different questions and neither corrects the other.
allLeagues.discovery: Discovery surfaces — recruitment, replacements, opportunities, similar players — do apply an evidence-aware ordering, and they show both numbers: the raw analytical value and the value the list was ordered by, with the reason. That ordering never changes the displayed percentile. Raw analytics and discovery ranking are kept apart on purpose.

scores.title: Intelligence scores
scores.what: Intelligence scores summarise a facet of play: ball progression, ball security, chance creation, defensive activity, duel dominance, 1v1 threat, goal threat, finishing and aerial presence.
scores.orderBefore: Component metrics are converted to percentiles
scores.orderAfter: being weighted, so quantities on different scales are never added together. The result is a 0 to 100 score. Component values are stored alongside the total, so any score can be decomposed into the metrics that produced it.
scores.inverted: Where a low value is good, such as being dispossessed or dribbled past, the percentile is inverted, so a higher score always reads as better within that facet.

roles.title: Player roles
roles.what: A role is a weighted combination of percentile metrics describing a style of player: a deep-lying playmaker weights progressive passing and retention, a ball-winning midfielder weights tackles, interceptions and duels.
roles.best: Every player is scored against each role compatible with their position group. The highest-scoring role is presented as their best statistical fit, with the alternatives shown beneath it.

similarity.title: Statistical similarity
similarity.body: Similarity compares players within a compatible position group using a position-specific feature vector. Features are standardised so that no single high-variance metric dominates, and the result is reported on a 0 to 100 Similarity Index.

sample.title: Sample size
sample.intro: All players with valid statistical data are included. Minutes do not determine eligibility. Sample labels indicate how much playing-time evidence supports the player's per-90 profile — nothing more.
sample.establishedRest: — established sample. Roughly ten full matches; per-90 figures are reasonably settled.
sample.developingRest: — developing sample. Enough football to read a direction from, though the rates still move.
sample.lowRest: — low sample. One goal or tackle moves a rate noticeably.
sample.veryLowRest: — very low sample. A per-90 from this little football is close to a single passage of play multiplied up. Read it as what happened, not as a rate the player sustains.
sample.arithmetic: The one requirement is arithmetic rather than editorial: a per-90 needs minutes to divide by. A player with no minutes behind a metric has no rate for it, and that metric reads N/A. Nothing is invented to fill the gap.

limits.heading: What these outputs do not mean
limits.notQuality: A role score measures statistical resemblance to a profile. A player can score 90 for a role and still be a poor signing: the score knows nothing about tactical fit, physical data, injury record, temperament, or what a scout sees.
limits.notProbability: The Similarity Index expresses closeness between two statistical profiles. It is not a likelihood that one player will reproduce the output of another.
limits.finishing: Goals above expected goals regresses heavily over the samples available within a single season. A high finishing score describes what happened, not a reliable measurement of finishing ability.
limits.notWorldRankingTitle: An all-leagues percentile is not a world ranking
limits.notWorldRanking: It is the rank of an observed per-90 value among the player-seasons currently served. No strength coefficient is applied, because an unvalidated one would introduce error while appearing authoritative; no season-maturity adjustment is applied, because it would replace an observed figure with a modelled one that a reader could not check against the per-90 printed beside it. Neither a high nor a low placement here is a verdict on a player.
limits.notFeeTitle: Market value is not a transfer fee
limits.notFee: Transfermarkt market values are crowd-sourced estimates rather than asking prices, and are used only as a rough affordability filter.
limits.goalkeepers: Basic goalkeeping statistics reflect the defence in front of the keeper as much as the keeper. Without a post-shot expected-goals metric, elite shot-stopping cannot be inferred from save percentage.

freshness.title: Data freshness
freshness.description: How often each source is refreshed.
freshness.batches: Provider APIs are never called while you browse. Data is ingested in scheduled batches, validated, transformed and only then published, so a failed or partial refresh cannot reach these pages.
freshness.publishedBefore: Published source freshness is reported on the
freshness.publishedAfter: page, and means the last dataset successfully promoted to production — not the last refresh attempted, and not the last time the checks ran. Those are listed separately, because a refresh can load into staging and never reach readers.
